typeName: Q3: Analyze an environmental problem with calculations
title: Irrigation: water use per area, efficiency and cost

stimulus.title: A farm considers switching from furrow to drip irrigation
stimulus.html:
Facts about the farm for one growing season (invented data for practice)
ItemValue
Area of the farm120 hectares
Water applied with furrow irrigation9,000 m³ per hectare
Efficiency of furrow irrigation (share of applied water the crop takes up)60%
Efficiency of drip irrigation90%
Price the farmer pays to pump water0.12 dollars per m³
Cost to install drip irrigation2,500 dollars per hectare

A 120-hectare farm in a dry valley grows vegetables with furrow irrigation. All of its water is pumped from an aquifer whose water table has dropped 20 meters in the last 30 years. The farmer is thinking about switching to drip irrigation. The crop would need the same amount of water under either method.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the total volume of water, in cubic meters, the farm applies in one season with furrow irrigation. Show your setup with units.

rubric.point: Correct setup: the area times the water applied per hectare, with units that cancel.
accept: An equivalent product that shows both values

parts.sample: Setup: 120 ha × 9,000 m³/ha = 1,080,000 m³ of water per season (1.08 × 10⁶ m³).

mistakes.why: 9,000 m³ is the water for one hectare. Multiply by the 120 hectares of the farm.
That is the water the crop takes up (60%). The question asks for all the water applied.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of water per hectare the farm would need to apply with drip irrigation to give the crop the same amount of water it takes up now. Show your setup.

rubric.point: Correct setup: the water the crop takes up (9,000 × 0.60) divided by the drip efficiency (0.90).
accept: An equivalent setup in two steps

rubric.point: Correct answer with units: 6,000 m³ per hectare.

parts.sample: The crop takes up 9,000 m³/ha × 0.60 = 5,400 m³/ha. With drip at 90% efficiency: 5,400 m³/ha ÷ 0.90 = 6,000 m³ per hectare.

mistakes.why: That is 90% of what is applied now. First find what the crop takes up (9,000 × 0.60), then divide by 0.90 for the water drip must apply.
Dividing by the efficiency gives the water you must apply. Multiplying by 0.90 gives less than the crop needs.
5,400 m³/ha is what the crop takes up. Drip loses 10%, so apply 5,400 ÷ 0.90.
8,100 is 90% of 9,000. Start from what the crop takes up, 5,400 m³/ha, and divide by 0.90.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate how much money, in dollars, the farm would save on water in one season by switching the whole farm to drip irrigation. Show your setup with units.

rubric.point: Correct setup: the water saved per hectare times the area times the price, with units that cancel. A value from an incorrect answer in (b) is used consistently.
Correct answer with units: 43,200 dollars (consistent with the answer to (b)).

parts.sample: Water saved: (9,000 - 6,000) m³/ha × 120 ha = 360,000 m³. Money saved: 360,000 m³ × 0.12 dollars/m³ = 43,200 dollars per season.

mistakes.why: 360 dollars is the saving on one hectare. Multiply by the 120 hectares.
That is the whole water bill with furrow irrigation. The saving is the difference between the two bills.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of years of water savings it would take to pay for installing drip irrigation on the whole farm. Show your setup.

rubric.point: Correct setup: the installation cost for the farm (2,500 dollars/ha × 120 ha) divided by the yearly saving from (c).
Correct answer with units: about 6.9 years (consistent with the answer to (c)).

parts.sample: Installation: 2,500 dollars/ha × 120 ha = 300,000 dollars. Payback: 300,000 dollars ÷ 43,200 dollars per year ≈ 6.9 years.

mistakes.why: 2,500 dollars is the cost for one hectare. Multiply by 120 hectares for the whole farm before dividing.
Put the cost on top: cost ÷ savings per year gives years.
That uses the cost of one hectare. The whole farm costs 2,500 × 120 = 300,000 dollars.
That is savings divided by cost. Years = cost ÷ savings per year.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Explain how years of furrow irrigation can lower the yield of the farm's soil through salinization.

rubric.point: A complete chain: irrigation water carries dissolved salts; water evaporates from the furrows and soil surface; the salt is left behind and builds up over years; salty soil makes it hard for roots to take up water, so yields fall.
accept: Water evaporates and leaves its dissolved salt in the soil; salt builds up and harms crops
Must name evaporation leaving salt behind; "the water is salty" alone does not earn the point

parts.sample: Even fresh well water carries a little dissolved salt. In furrow irrigation, much of the water evaporates from the furrows and the soil surface; only the water leaves, so the salt stays in the topsoil. Season after season the salt builds up, and roots in salty soil struggle to take up water, so the crop grows less and yields fall.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: The aquifer under the valley is shared by many farms. Propose a policy that the state could adopt to slow the drop in the water table, and explain how it would work.

rubric.point: A law or rule (not a technology) fitted to the shared aquifer, with how it works: e.g., a law that caps the volume each well may pump per year, with meters, so total pumping stays at or below recharge; or a fee per cubic meter pumped, so farms use less.
accept: A state law limiting each farm's yearly pumping (with meters), so withdrawals no longer exceed recharge
A charge for each cubic meter pumped, so farms save water to save money
A subsidy for drip irrigation paid for by the state, with how it lowers pumping
Naming drip irrigation alone, with no law or rule, does not earn the point

parts.sample: The state could pass a law that requires a meter on every irrigation well and caps how many cubic meters each farm may pump per hectare each year. Because the caps are set so that total pumping is no more than the rain and snowmelt that recharge the aquifer, the water table would stop falling.
